title: Hud and 'Ad
hookLine: Hud warns the builders of high towers, and the wind comes (7:65–72)

lines: EVERY AGE HAS ITS TALLEST BUILDING.
cards: Cities race each other for the tallest building, and boast when they win. Glass towers, stone walls, a bigger house, a bigger bank balance, a big following. Building isn't wrong.
But sometimes people build not to shelter anyone, only to feel that nothing can touch them.
The Qur'an tells of an ancient Arabian people called 'Ad, well-known for their strength and their building, and of a man from among them sent to warn them. His name was Hud.

teach.b: Surah seven, verse sixty-five, introduces him simply: to 'Ad, their brother Hud. Not a stranger; one of their own. His message is the one Nuh brought just before him: my people, worship Allah, you have no god but Him.

He reminds them that Allah made them successors after the people of Nuh and gave them great stature and strength. The chiefs call him a fool and a liar, and say they won't leave what their fathers worshipped.
Other surahs fill in the picture.

teach.h: A LANDMARK ON EVERY HIGH PLACE.
teach.b: In surah twenty-six, Hud asks: do you build a landmark on every high place, just for show, and fortresses, as if you'll live forever? In surah forty-one, they boast: who is mightier than us in strength?
Surah eighty-nine names their city Iram, of the lofty pillars. Then the end.

teach.h: A CLOUD THEY THOUGHT WAS RAIN.
teach.b: Surah forty-six says they saw a cloud coming toward their valleys and said, this cloud will bring us rain. It wasn't rain.
Surah sixty-nine calls it a furious, roaring wind, sent against them for seven nights and eight days, until they lay like the hollow trunks of palm trees.
Surah seven says simply that Allah saved Hud and those with him, and cut off the rest. Where were they?
Surah forty-six places them at al-Ahqaf, the sand dunes, which commentators set in southern Arabia; beyond that, the sources don't say for certain. The lesson doesn't need the map.
Towers, pillars, strength: none of it was safety.

how: Muslims honor Hud as a prophet sent to the Arabian people of 'Ad; surah eleven bears his name, and teachers read his story as a warning against trusting strength and wealth instead of God.

o: the prophet sent to his own people, 'Ad
the builder of the lofty pillars of Iram
the wind that came for seven nights

games.q: the story across surahs — tap the pairs.
p: a landmark on every high place
a cloud they thought was rain
seven nights and eight days of wind

s: the Qur'an calls Hud the brother of 'Ad
to 'Ad, their brother Hud: one of their own.
'Ad saw the cloud and feared it
they said, this cloud will bring us rain.
the Qur'an gives exact coordinates for 'Ad
it names al-Ahqaf, the dunes; commentators place it in southern Arabia, and more is uncertain.

games.q: you're one of 'Ad, and a dark cloud rolls toward your valley after a long dry spell. what did they say?
o: this cloud will bring us rain.
games.why: they welcomed it as rain. surah 46 says it was the very thing they had asked to hurry: a wind with a painful punishment.

practice: Ask yourself honestly what you build to feel strong: savings, a title, a reputation, a body at the gym, the people who'd take your side. None of these is bad, so pick one and hold it in mind.
Then ask what would still hold you up if it were gone tomorrow, and stay with whatever answer comes, even a quiet one.

wordCard.voice: Hud. A prophet sent to his own people, the great builders of ancient Arabia, 'Ad, who trusted their strength until the wind came. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: Hud, the prophet sent to 'Ad; surah eleven is named for him.

carryVoice: Your line: towers aren't safety. Strength was never the shelter. That's day four hundred nine.
